opus-5.5.text:
I think it's changed things quite a lot, honestly. When I was younger, especially as a student, I had this feeling that health was something you could borrow against. You stay up late, you skip meals, you sit in front of the screen for twelve hours, and your body just kind of absorbs it. And for a while it does. But once you're working at a place where the pace is really intense, where you're shipping things, debugging training runs at odd hours, and the work never really "ends," you start to notice that your output is directly tied to how you feel physically.

There were periods where I was working very long stretches, and I could tell my thinking got worse. Not dramatically, but you make more small mistakes, you're slower to see the bug, you get irritable in discussions. And in this kind of work, clarity of thinking is basically the whole job. So I started seeing exercise and sleep less as a "nice to have" and more as part of the work itself. If I want to be productive over years, not just over one sprint, I have to maintain the machine.

So now I try to be pretty deliberate about it. Regular exercise, even if it's just going to the gym or running a few times a week, trying not to sacrifice sleep unless something is truly urgent. And I think it's also about sustainability. A lot of people in this field are very passionate and they'll burn themselves out because the problems are so exciting. But it's a long game. The people who do great work over a career are usually the ones who figured out how to keep going without breaking down.

So yeah, I'd say the intensity actually made me take health more seriously, not less. It's kind of the foundation that everything else sits on.

r001.rationale: Jiayi says the intense pace made her recognize the need to sustain her health, describing work as a long game and the risk of burning out or breaking down.

r002.rationale: The response mentions running a few times a week, but says nothing about a 3,000-meter PE run at Tsinghua or contrasting past inability with current voluntary practice.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's changed everything. When I was working on things like Tianshou back in school, and then later at OpenAI during the really intense stretches, I had this mindset that sleep and exercise were basically overhead. Like, every hour at the gym was an hour I wasn't fixing a bug or running an experiment. And for a while you can get away with that, because you're young and the adrenaline carries you.

But what I found is that the quality of my thinking degraded way before I noticed it. I'd be debugging something at 2 a.m., convinced I was being productive, and then the next morning I'd look at the code and realize I'd made it worse. The mistakes I made when I was exhausted cost more time than the exercise ever would have.

So now I treat it as infrastructure. I go to the gym regularly, I try to sleep properly, and I'm pretty strict about it even when there's a deadline. Maybe especially when there's a deadline. Running or lifting is also the one time my brain isn't trying to solve something, and weirdly that's often when the solution shows up. I've had a lot of "oh, that's obviously the problem" moments halfway through a run.

The other thing is that this work is a marathon. The people I admire most in this field are the ones who have been doing it consistently for ten, fifteen years, not the ones who burned bright for two. If I want to still be useful in a decade, I can't keep spending down my health like it's free. It's not.

r001.rationale: She says the intense schedule changed everything and that spending down her health was not free; she now protects sleep and exercise to remain useful over the long term, communicating that the schedule was unsustainable.

r002.rationale: The response mentions running as exercise, but says nothing about a 3,000-meter PE run at Tsinghua or a contrast between then and now.

astra-6.text: An intense work schedule has made me realize that health can’t just be something I take care of when I have extra time. When work gets busy, exercise is often the first thing you cut, but that’s also when you need a way to step back and recharge. I’ve started to see it less as something that competes with work and more as something that helps me keep going. Even if I can’t fit in a full workout, making time to move feels important. For me, it’s about building a routine I can sustain, instead of pushing hard and then having to recover.

r001.rationale: The response says a sustainable routine matters, but does not state that the intense work schedule itself was unsustainable.

r002.rationale: It mentions fitting in exercise generally, but says nothing about a 3,000-meter PE run at Tsinghua or voluntarily running that distance now.

sol-6.1.text: An intense work schedule has made me realize that health can’t always be the thing I put off until I have more time. When I’m busy, it’s easy to sacrifice sleep or skip exercise, but then I have less energy and find it harder to focus. So I’ve started seeing exercise as part of taking care of myself, rather than something extra. Even if I can only make time for a short walk, that still matters. I want to be able to sustain the work I care about, and that means taking my health seriously.
